Section 01

From Sample to Confidence Interval

01
CHEM 3400H

Population parameters vs sample statistics

{{ term.symbol }}
{{ term.label }}
{{ term.desc }}
We never know the true population parameters: every sampling plan is an attempt to estimate them from a finite number of samples.
CHEM 3400H

Why do replicate samples never agree exactly?

Repeated observations vary because of random effects. Instrumental and preparation noise remain even for stable homogeneous material; independent field samples can also differ because of spatial or temporal heterogeneity and subsampling.
As n increases, the standard error of the mean decreases. Under common conditions, the Central Limit Theorem also makes the sampling distribution of the mean increasingly close to normal.
{{ revealCLT.prompt }}
SE = s / √n
The standard error of the mean shrinks with the SQUARE ROOT of n, not n itself. Quadrupling the number of samples only halves the uncertainty: a law of diminishing returns you must weigh against cost.
CHEM 3400H

The confidence interval for a sample mean

CI = x̄ ± (t* · s / √n)
x̄ = sample mean  ·  s = sample standard deviation  ·  n = number of independent observations  ·  t* = critical value from the t-distribution at n−1 degrees of freedom and the chosen confidence level.
{{ revealCI.prompt }}
When the population standard deviation σ is unknown, we estimate it with the sample standard deviation s and use the t-distribution. This matters especially for small samples, where s is a more uncertain estimate of σ. As the degrees of freedom increase, the t-distribution approaches the normal (z) distribution.
CHEM 3400H

Worked example: five replicate measurements of a water sample give a mean of 12.4 mg/L, s = 0.6 mg/L. Find the two-sided 95% CI (t* = 2.776, df = 4).

{{ step.prompt }}
{{ step.answer }}
CHEM 3400H

What a 95% confidence interval does not mean

A 95% CI does not mean "95% of individual measurements fall in this range." It means: if you repeated this entire sampling and analysis process many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true population mean.
The interval describes your uncertainty about where the true mean lies, not the spread of the raw data, which is instead described by the standard deviation, s, directly.
CHEM 3400H
Section 02

How Many Samples Do You Need?

02
CHEM 3400H

Working backward: solving for the number of samples, n

n₀ = (z · s₀ / E)²
E = target margin of error; s₀ = planning estimate of the population standard deviation. This z-based expression gives an initial sample-size estimate; always round up.
{{ revealN.prompt }}
For a small-sample t interval, refine the initial estimate because t* depends on n through df = n − 1. Recalculate with the corresponding t* until the rounded-up n no longer changes.
Also note: n scales with s² and inversely with E², so a noisier population or a tighter precision target both demand rapidly more samples.
CHEM 3400H

Diminishing returns, drawn out

CHEM 3400H

Where does the s in the sample-size equation come from?

The sample-size equation needs an estimate of s before you have collected your real samples, which seems circular. In practice, this comes from a small pilot study, a limited round of preliminary sampling, historical data from a similar site or matrix, or a conservative literature estimate.
An underestimated pilot s leads to an undersized plan that fails to hit its target margin of error; a badly overestimated s wastes resources oversampling. Pilot data quality directly controls how good the resulting plan is.
CHEM 3400H

Diminishing returns: doubling n does not halve the interval

nRelative half-width (fixed critical value; ∝ 1/√n)% reduction from n=3 31.00× - 60.71×29% 120.50×50% 240.35×65% 480.25×75%
Beyond a certain point, each additional sample buys progressively less precision for its cost. This is why sampling plans target a specific, justified E rather than "as many as possible."

Section 03

Outliers and Composite Variance

03
CHEM 3400H

Should you reject a suspicious data point? The Q-test

Qexp = gap / range
gap = |suspect extreme − nearest value|  ·  range = highest − lowest. For the chosen Dixon-Q variant, confidence level, and n, reject the no-outlier null hypothesis only when Qexp > Qcritical. The usual simple Q-test screens one suspected extreme value in approximately normal data.
{{ revealQ.prompt }}
A statistical test is not a substitute for investigating why a point looks unusual. Document the investigation and follow the approved QC plan; do not repeatedly test and remove values or discard a result simply because it is inconvenient.
CHEM 3400H

Worked example: replicate results (mg/L) are 4.01, 4.03, 4.02, 4.15. Is 4.15 an outlier? (Qcritical, n=4, 90% = 0.76)

{{ step.prompt }}
{{ step.answer }}

Compositing reduces variance, but hides information

Why compositing helps

For k independent, equal-mass increments that are completely mixed, the variance of the composite mean is approximately σ²/k. This reduces between-increment variance in the reported average, but one analysis still has its own preparation and analytical variance.

What compositing loses

A composite gives you the AVERAGE across its sub-samples, but destroys any information about the maximum, the range, or which sub-location was the worst offender: a critical loss when the regulatory question is "is there a hot spot," not "what is the average."

CHEM 3400H

Worked example: compositing four sub-samples

Suppose four independent, equal-mass soil increments each have a between-increment variance of 16 (mg/kg)². What happens to the variance when they are composited?
Step 1: Identify the averaging relationship
For k independent, equal-mass increments, the variance of the composite mean is σ²/k.
Step 2: Calculate the composite variance
σ²/k = 16/4 = 4 (mg/kg)². The corresponding standard deviation is √4 = 2 mg/kg, before preparation and analytical variance are added.
Step 3: Interpret the trade-off
Compositing reduces variance in the reported average, but it also hides the individual result. A hot spot in one of the four increments could disappear into the composite value.
CHEM 3400H

90%, 95%, or 99%: the confidence level is a choice, not a rule

95% confidence is the default convention in most analytical chemistry, but it is a convention, not a law of nature. A higher confidence level (99%) widens the interval and demands more samples for the same margin of error; a lower one (90%) narrows it but accepts more risk of missing the true mean.
Regulatory and legal contexts often specify the required confidence level explicitly; where they do not, the choice should reflect the real-world cost of being wrong.
CHEM 3400H
Section 04

Check Your Understanding

04
CHEM 3400H

Why n − 1, not n?

Degrees of freedom represent how many values are genuinely free to vary once the sample mean is fixed. With n data points and a calculated mean, only n − 1 of them can vary independently, the last one is determined by the others and the mean.
This is why a one-sample t interval uses df = n − 1: with smaller n, s is a less certain estimate of σ and the t critical value is larger. The Dixon Q-test is different: its critical value is indexed by sample size n and the selected test variant, not by n − 1 degrees of freedom.

CHEM 3400H
Key Takeaways

Precision has a price, and statistics tells you what it is

  • A confidence interval quantifies uncertainty in a sample mean as an estimate of the target population mean.
  • Standard error shrinks with √n, not n: each added sample buys progressively less precision.
  • A planning estimate of variability and a target margin of error let you estimate sample size before collection, then refine it for the intended interval.
  • The Q-test can screen one suspected extreme value under specific assumptions, but it never replaces investigation and documented QC rules.
  • Compositing reduces variance but destroys spatial and maximum-value information: choose it only when the average is the actual question.
